analysis.one_liner: Expands oil, gas, coal, and mining production on federal land while waiving environmental reviews and repealing clean-energy programs.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors and never left the Senate Energy Committee, dying without a hearing or vote as the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the Interior Department to hold far more oil and gas lease sales on federal lands and waters every year, cut royalties companies pay, and limit the president's ability to slow or stop drilling, fracking, and pipelines. It would shorten or waive environmental reviews for energy and mining projects, repeal the fee on methane leaks from oil and gas systems, and eliminate federal programs that pay homeowners to make their homes more energy efficient. Supporters called it a way to lower energy prices; opponents called it a gift to fossil fuel producers.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies get more federal land and water opened to leasing with lower royalties, faster permits, and no methane emissions charge. Coal and mining companies get easier permitting and fewer ways for the public or agencies to delay projects. LNG exporters and pipeline builders get streamlined approvals and the removal of presidential permit authority over border-crossing projects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil, gas, coal, and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Department to hold at least four onshore oil and gas lease sales per year in each of nine states and at least two offshore sales per year in the Gulf of Mexico and Alaska regions, offering all nominated parcels [S3].
Cuts the royalties companies pay for oil and gas extracted from federal land and eliminates the charge on methane emissions from petroleum and natural gas systems [S2][S3].

Waives or shortens environmental review requirements under laws like the National Environmental Policy Act for energy projects, limits agencies' ability to delay federal land energy development, and bars the president from declaring a fracking moratorium without an act of Congress [S2].

Removes the requirement that pipeline projects get state water quality certifications under federal water law and replaces presidential permits for cross-border pipelines and power lines with a faster FERC process [S3].
Repeals the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, the high-efficiency electric home rebate program, home energy efficiency contractor training grants, and building energy code assistance [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near drilling, mining, and pipeline routes get less say and fewer environmental reviews before projects are built. Taxpayers lose federal royalty revenue from lower charges on companies extracting public resources. Homeowners lose rebates that offset the cost of heat pumps and efficiency upgrades, and the public bears the air, water, and climate effects of expanded production.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the home energy rebate and efficiency programs would take away direct household help — the Inflation Reduction Act programs that paid homeowners for electric appliances and efficiency upgrades — which sits oddly in a bill titled to lower energy costs [S3].

Cutting royalties and eliminating the methane emissions charge shifts costs onto taxpayers: companies would pay less for extracting publicly owned oil and gas while the public absorbs the air and water impacts [S2][S3].

Waiving environmental reviews, charging fees to file protests against lease sales, and limiting agencies' authority to delay projects would leave nearby residents with less notice, less scrutiny, and fewer legal tools before drilling or mining begins [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main beneficiaries are the companies that lease and extract federal energy resources, not households; the provisions that would directly touch consumer energy costs are the repeal of home efficiency rebates, which removes help rather than adding it. Any effect on pump or utility prices from expanded leasing would be slow and uncertain, while the environmental and revenue costs are concrete. On balance the bill transfers public resources and regulatory protection to a specific industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. John Kennedy introduced the bill in the Senate on March 22, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1][S5].
No other action followed — the committee never reported it, and it never received a vote [S5].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor during the two-year Congress [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it never advanced, existing environmental review requirements, the methane emissions charge, the lower federal royalty debate, and the home energy rebate programs all remained in place; the oil, gas, coal, and mining interests that would have gained from the bill got nothing from the Senate version.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept existing safeguards; industry gains never came

for.name: Sen. John Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Joe Manchin (D) in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill, leaving it without any committee action for two years.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever recorded on this bill, but its single Republican sponsor attracted no cosponsors of either party in a chamber where Democrats held the committee chairs and the floor agenda.

industries.note: Mandatory lease sales, lower royalties, a repealed methane charge, and fast-tracked permits would directly raise company profits from public lands while cutting federal revenue and weakening the review process nearby communities rely on. The industry's gain in this bill runs directly against the public's stake in clean air, water, and fair returns on public resources.

The bill mandates coal leasing, speeds permitting for mines including uranium, and bars agencies from delaying mineral development on federal land. Less scrutiny before mining on public land transfers risk to surrounding communities and taxpayers stuck with cleanup.

The bill deems natural gas exports automatically in the public interest, removes state water quality certification and presidential permits for cross-border pipelines, and sets hard deadlines that agencies must meet or explain to Congress. Faster approvals and fewer community checks mean faster build-out of export infrastructure.

The bill repeals the home energy rebate program and contractor training grants, programs that created customer demand for heat pumps, insulation, and electric upgrades. Contractors and homeowners were on the same side in opposing this repeal.
